related_questions.question: Is it okay to live with piles?
related_questions.snippet: Living a normal life with piles is entirely possible with the right management and treatment. Piles, also known as hemorrhoids, can often be managed with lifestyle changes such as incorporating a high-fiber diet, staying well-hydrated, and avoiding prolonged sitting or straining during bowel movements.

related_questions.question: Do and don'ts in piles?
related_questions.snippet: If you have hemorrhoids, you should avoid foods that are fatty or low in fiber: These foods encourage constipation, which can cause more pain and bleeding. Foods to avoid include dairy, meat, and processed foods. Doctors recommend a high-fiber diet. Soluble fiber makes well-formed, soft stools that are easy to pass.

related_questions.question: Do piles go away on their own?
related_questions.snippet: Haemorrhoids (piles) often clear up by themselves after a few days. However, there are many treatments that can reduce itching and discomfort. Making simple dietary changes and not straining on the toilet are often recommended first.

text_blocks.snippet: Piles, also known as hemorrhoids, are swollen veins in the rectum or anus. Common symptoms of piles include:

list.snippet: Rectal bleeding: Bright red blood on toilet paper, in the stool, or dripping into the toilet bowl
Pain and discomfort: Especially during bowel movements or when sitting
Swelling and lumps: Visible or palpable lumps around the anus
Itching and irritation: Around the anus
Protruding hemorrhoids: Internal hemorrhoids may bulge out of the anus, especially during straining
Constipation: Piles can contribute to difficulty passing stools
Mucus discharge: Clear or yellowish mucus may leak from the anus
Difficulty sitting or standing: Severe piles can make it uncomfortable to sit or stand for prolonged periods
Urinary problems: In rare cases, piles can cause urinary difficulties
Fever and chills: If piles become infected
